utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Given the weather out, I wish I could say we had another gap in our witnesses but as you can see before you, we have our next witness. It's Ari Kerkkanen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. I guess I'll deal with the housekeeping at the end of the witness's testimony. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kerkkanen. You may take a seat. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Could you just state your name, please, for the record.

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: My name is Ari Kerkkanen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkkanen, obviously we both speak English. For the benefit of the interpreters it's important that, number 1, we don't speak too quickly, number 2, that we insert a pause between question and answer. So when I finish my question just pause for a moment before you answer and I'll try to remember to do the same when you finish your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'd like to pass out a statement of the witness. We have copies of the statement in English for the Trial Chamber. We also have B/C/S versions for Defence counsel and the accused. While it's being passed out, I can say that it had, pursuant to the Trial Chamber's order of last week, the 28th of April 2006, the statement has been redacted as ordered by the Trial Chamber, and the annex, the heading that was missing from the annex has been inserted so I believe we've complied with the order of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know whether members of the Trial Chamber were present when that was done are able to confirm what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This was a written order that came out on the 28th of April 2006. We tried to carefully do the redactions that were ordered by the Trial Chamber but if it's found that we made a -- any error, then, of course, that will be corrected. But I'm pretty sure we got it right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkkanen, could you look at that document that's in front of you and first of all can you tell us whether this is your statement and the -- annex 1 being your report and annex 2 being a spreadsheet containing documents?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes. This is my witness statement, with basically two annexes. Annex 1 is the review of documentary evidence on Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina and Republic of Serbian Krajina Ministry of Internal Affairs and annex 2 is basically exhibit chart on documentary evidence on which annex 1 was based on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I noticed that Your Honour's microphone is on by --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a few questions about this -- about this document before I offer it into evidence. In paragraph 2 of your statement, which is just the second page after the cover sheet, it states that you joined the ICTY on the 22nd of November 2002 as a criminal intelligence analyst. Are you still employed in that position?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: No, not any more. I left the ICTY on the 5th of July 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And after you left the ICTY where did you go in terms of work?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: I was working -- after I left the ICTY, I was working as a political adviser to the multi-national task force north, EUFOR, in Bosnia-Herzegovina until the end of November 2005, and since the beginning of this year, 2006, I have been working as a researcher at the University of Helsinki.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, the task force that you worked for the multi-national task force known as EUFOR, that's spelled E-U-F-O-R, when you were working with them, where were you based?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: I was based at camp eagle base, that is EUFOR base very close to the town of Tuzla in the northern part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kerkkanen, before coming today to testify, did you have an opportunity again to review your statement, your attached report, and all of the documents cited in your report?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes, I had an opportunity to review them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in the process of doing that review, did you have a few corrections or amendments to make to your statement and to your report?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes. I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd like to go through those now, if we may. First, on page 3 of your statement, in paragraphs 10 through 14, you describe five different document missions that you undertook with others from the Tribunal. Was there an additional document mission after this report -- after this statement and the report were completed?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes. There was one more additional mission that took place in the beginning of June 2005, to Petrinja, an archive collection of the Croatian state archives, basically the collection is located in Petrinja in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, could we look, please, at footnote 231 of your report, which is annex 1 to your statement? It's on page 59 of the English. And at that footnote it says "underlying evidence will be provided when confidentiality is lifted." Can you explain what that means and why that phrase was included in the footnote?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes. While I was writing this report, and statement, this particular document was still placed under Rule 70 restriction, and therefore I couldn't put more details about this document into the footnote, but I understand that the confidentiality of this document was later lifted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at 65 ter Exhibit 1491? Could we have that on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkkanen, are you able to see that -- are you able to see that document and is it big enough for you to read?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is this the document that you were referring to in footnote 231?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Is it possible to see a little bit more of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, if we could scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes. I can confirm that this is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what the source of the document is, how it was obtained by the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: I know that this document has been obtained by one of the OTP's investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And from -- and do you know how the investigator obtained it?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: From one of his witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I'm done with that document, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you are done with the document, I assume that your opposite number has a B/C/S copy of this as we are looking at the English copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the way this should work is the -- because the witness speaks English, the Defence can look at the same document on B/C/S on their monitors. The B/C/S version of the document should come up on their monitors and they can, of course, confirm for us if that's what has happened. But that's how it should happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you confirm, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have the English version. We recognise the document but it's in English. Mr. Martic, however, cannot understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, there may need the assistance of technical personnel but they should be able to open up their -- not the courtroom screen but their individual monitor, you can open up the e-court and pick the language of the document and if they pick B/C/S then the document should come up in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please check with Mr. Martic's screen to see whether he's got the B/C/S on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to inform you that we do have the document in B/C/S, but we have to find it in e-court to avoid any misunderstandings. We have no problem with this document. It can be found in e-court in B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Milovancevic, and thank you very much for your consideration but I would like to be sure that Mr. Martic is up to speed and is not left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Martic does not have the document before him in B/C/S. That is a technical problem we have at present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I'm advised that a technician is coming to help Mr. Martic with that problem. Let's hope that it will be resolved fairly soon. Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There will be -- I won't be looking at any more documents for a little bit so perhaps that will give time for that problem to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could turn back to the report which is annex 1 of your statement and turn to page 60, please, it's page 60 in the English. For the B/C/S it's just at the end of the section 3.1. I can't say precisely which page it's on but it's at the end of section 3.1. There is a sentence there at the top of the page which states, "A report from RSK MUP special unit administration to MUP Serbia in July 1995 states that six Serbian MUP members were killed in action in the RSK." Is there a mistake in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. When I was reviewing again these documents, I realised that there is a mistake, and this last sentence or the end of the sentence should read that six Serbian MUP members were wounded in action in the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, let's look, please, at annex 2, which is entitled, "Exhibit chart on documentary evidence on Serbian autonomous region of Krajina, SAO Krajina, and Republic of Serbian Krajina, RSK, Ministry of Internal Affairs MUP." Now my first question about this annex is, just to be clear, are the documents that are listed on the spreadsheet that is here in annex 2 all documents that are cited in your report?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes. This is exactly the case. All documents I was referring to are in annex 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, on this spreadsheet, in the column on the far right-hand side there is a field for the source or what you've called the origin of the exhibit. Could you tell us, please, how did you determine the origins of these various exhibits?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: There is a one way of determining it, and that's so-called MIIF evidence record or tracking system that is in place in the Tribunal. MIIF abbreviation stands for mini information index form, and it means that each and every evidence irrespective of the type of evidence that is brought into the Tribunal will be MIIFed, meaning given a specific evidence number and in this MIIF record also the source or origin of the evidence is written, as well as who brought it into the Tribunal wherefrom it was obtained so I was using this MIIF database or record database in order to determine origin of these documents, but in addition of this, of course, many documents cited in my report were from those document missions I was carrying out, and therefore for those documents I knew that they are from those specific archives or document collections.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, just for our benefit, could you describe, please, the various ways just generally that documents that the documents that are cited in this annex were obtained by the OTP in this case?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: There are at least four different ways of -- for OTP to obtain documents. Of course, the first one is as it was used in this case and in writing this report with those so-called document missions when a team of analysts, investigators, from the OTP went physically to visit archives and document holdings and retrieved some documents from there. This is one way. The second is -- was -- is -- or was to send a request for assistance for various institutions or governments and asking for some specific documents or document collections. The third is that OTP investigators sometimes get documents from their witnesses and the fourth basically are open-source documents like newspaper articles or similar. So basically these four ways of obtaining documents were used also in writing this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you about some of the sources that you cite here, which may be not completely familiar to us. If you could look, please, for the source for footnote 7, 65 ter Exhibit 2033, the source there is Glasnik Krajine. Could you tell us what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: There is open source, meaning a newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if you look at -- thank you. For footnote 8, 65 ter Exhibit 47, you have listed there as a source, Amir Ahmic, office of the Bosniak liaison officer to the ICTY. Could you explain that source, please?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Basically it means that this document has been obtained from the Bosnian government. This person is a liaison officer by the Bosnian government to the ICTY and most likely the document has been obtained through RFA, request for assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know by the way -- those requests for assistance, are they made pursuant to the Statute and Rules of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you about the source for footnote 9, 65 ter Exhibit 55. You have there listed Orsat Miljanic Croatian Office for Cooperation. In other places, you have a reference just to the Croatia Office for Cooperation. For example, on the next page of this spreadsheet that can be seen. Could you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes. It's basically exactly the same situation than with the previous one except for the fact that these documents have been obtained from the Croatian government through their office of cooperation with the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in item -- for footnote 10, rather, 65 ter Exhibit 1960, the source is Croatian state archive, Zagreb, Croatia. Could you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: There was a quite a significant amount of SAO Krajina and RS Krajina documentation that was held by the Croatian Ministry of Defence and the Croatian counterintelligence agency. This material was transferred in 2004, perhaps a part of it even a little bit before, to the possession of the Croatian state archives in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And were some of your document missions that you describe in your statement to do searches of the Croatian state archives in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes. We had at least two extensive missions of two weeks of each to the Croatian state archives in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in footnote -- for footnote 11, 65 ter Exhibit 2035 the reference is to Narodne Novine. First of all before I ask you what that is, I forgot to ask you, do you speak B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: I have an intermediate knowledge of B/C/S due to my studies of this language at the University of Helsinki.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now back to this source Narodne Novine can you tell us what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: This is an Official Gazette of SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What do you mean by that, an Official Gazette of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: An official paper or newspaper where all laws that were promulgated were published.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in footnote 18, 65 ter 1943 the source is Sluzbeni Glasnik RS Krajina. Could you tell us what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: This is Official Gazette of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In item 45, rather footnote 45, and specifically 65 ter 1999, you have as the source RH MUP. What is that a reference to, please?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: This reference is to the Republic of Croatia Ministry of the Interior, Republika Hrvatska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we look at footnote 66, 65 ter Exhibit 1902, the source is the Banja Luka CSB. Could you explain what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: This means Banja Luka security service centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At footnote 106, 65 ter 1256, the source is Goran Granic, president of the council for cooperation with the ICTY. Can you explain what that source is, please?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: This source is -- means also that the document has been obtained from the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Looking now at footnote 127, 65 ter Exhibit 715 -- I mean, sorry, 716, the source there is -- it says DKPO. Should it read DPKO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are testifying. You should ask him what it should read.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, I'm sorry, I led him on this because I thought it was not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But why don't you tell us, Mr. Kerkkanen, what's there and what you think should be there and what it means.

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: When I was reviewing this annex 2 I realised there was a mistake in this abbreviation. It means peacekeeping department of the UN, so it's a UN source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But is the acronym correct as it stands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you correct it, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should read PKDO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: PKDO. Which means? Peacekeeping department of? What did you say, the full name, peacekeeping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, I do not recall. It's -- I know this department. It's UN peacekeeping department for -- I'm not -- Your Honour, I'm not sure about the exact name of this department but I know that it stands for UN peacekeeping department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That will suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could look at footnote 143, 65 ter 1352, there are a number of documents for footnote 143 but it's the last one, 65 ter 1352, source that's listed there is 1 KKVRS. Could you tell us what that means, please?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: It means the 1st Krajina Corps of Republic of Serbia in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and its army Vojska [Realtime transcript read in error "was"] Republika Srpska, the army of the Republic of Serbia in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Not to confuse with the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay just so we are clear, what does VRS stand for again?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: It stands for the Bosnian Serb army in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But what are the initials stand for? You said it but it didn't get recorded. You said it in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: The initials stand for Vojska Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, elsewhere, there is a reference to the 1 KK Banja Luka. For example, footnote 195, 65 ter Exhibit 707. What is that?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: It's the same corps, the 1st Krajina Corps in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, looking at footnote 215, 65 ter Exhibit 1901, the source that's listed is RS MUP CJB Sprsko Sarajevo, Pale. Can you explain what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: This is public security centre of Serbian Sarajevo, located in Pale, and of Republika Srpska MUP, meaning Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Looking at footnote 236, 65 ter Exhibit 2031, the source is Zlatan Ramic, AID Sarajevo, and in other -- other documents, for example, footnote 256, footnote 257, there is an a source reference to AID Sarajevo. Can you explain what this is a reference to, please?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: This reference is to basically to the Bosnian government and to their intelligence agency. So these documents have been obtained from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: A number of sources that the source is listed as OTP investigator, for example, footnote 258, 259, 260 and others, which is on the next-to-last page of the document, can you explain what that is a reference to, please?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes. Basically it's one of those ways our OTP has obtained documents, meaning that the OTP investigator has received documents from his or her witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to turn, please, to the page that has footnotes 136, 137, 138 and 140. And if you'll see on that page, for those footnotes that I just read out, there is no source listed. It simply says, delayed disclosure, though the documents are identified by 65 ter number, 2039, 2099, 2100.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours just to be clear those documents have now, of course, been disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkkanen, with respect to those three documents, 2039, 2099 and 2100, do you know what the source of those documents is?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes. I know the source of these documents is Petrinja archive collection of the Croatian state archives but at the time when I was writing this report, we didn't have a confirmed information about their exact origin, and for this end, we put a request for assistance to the Croatian government, requesting to have these three particular documents and the place of their origin. We received as a response to our RFA, these documents that were coming from the Petrinja archive collection and then later, on my mission to this particular collection in June of 2005, I double checked that these documents were in that archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, looking at the footnote 223, 65 ter Exhibit 260, the source that you have there is Diana Dicklich in trial support, and the document is described as an ECMM document. First of all, can you explain what is ECMM and second, explain why the source is listed that way?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: ECMM stands for European Community Monitoring Mission. That is a civilian monitoring mission reporting to the council of European Union, and it was deployed in the area of the former Yugoslavia already I think in the end of 1991 or from the beginning of 1992, and this mission has been -- is known nowadays, from the beginning of year 2002, as European Union Monitoring Mission, EUMM. Obviously, this document from ECMM, which headquarters by the way is in Sarajevo, has been obtained through an RFA to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So what should be the source listed for that document, just to be clear?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: It should read ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kerkkanen, aside from these changes and corrections that we have made today to your statement, annex 1 and annex 2 of the statement, is everything in these documents true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, pursuant to the Court's ruling of last week, 28 April 2006, I'd move into evidence now this statement and the two annexes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The statement is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. And the statement is admitted together with its two annexes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 459, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And does the exhibit number combine the statement and the annexes?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkkanen, in addition to the documents that are contained in the spreadsheet that is annex 2, did you review other documents during your document missions and while writing this report?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you give us some idea of the volume of documents that you reviewed, tens, hundreds, thousands?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Perhaps it gives a kind of idea about the volume of this material, as I say, that on those six document missions we carried out, we selected about 20.000 pages of documents, that is approximately as I counted, about 3.000 different documents, but this is a very small amount of the whole of -- of whole documentation we were reviewing on those missions. So what we are talking here, if we are talking about the whole documentation of the SAO Krajina or RSK documentation in Croatia it's hundreds of thousands of pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, did you yourself review hundreds of thousands of pages or was that done by more people than yourself?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Our team of reviewers consisted always at least from at least two reviewers but usually more than two, from two to five analysts and investigators so my estimation by myself I reviewed between 50 to 100.000 pages of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, based on your review of all of those documents, is there anything -- did you see anything in the documents that are contained in annex 2 of your report that would cause you to doubt the authenticity of those documents?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now I'd like to show you another spreadsheet and make it available to the Trial Chamber and to the parties, with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour this is a spreadsheet I'm really going to be using for logistical reason, to move documents into evidence. It will make it, for reasons that should become clear very quickly it will make it easier to use this spreadsheet. This spreadsheet obviously, closely, is identical to the annex 2 with some differences and I'll just explain what the differences are, if I may. And this is not relevant to the testimony. This is just -- this is just to -- this is just mechanics to get the documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, where documents have already been admitted into evidence in the case, that's indicated on this spreadsheet. Secondly, there were some -- on the original annex two spreadsheet there are a number of indications where it's a translation in progress, and there was no ERN number for the translation. Obviously those translations have been completed and in this spreadsheet the ERN of the translation has been included. Third, there is a -- one document, it's for entry 150, it's 65 ter Exhibit 2000 that we'll seek admission under seal and that's indicated on the spreadsheet for the benefit of the court officer. Finally there are three entries that are deleted from the annex 2 spreadsheet. Those entries are 3, 5, and 88. The reason for that is 3 and 5 both, as you can see from the annex 2 spreadsheet, both refer to an expert report in another case. We didn't think that it was appropriate to seek admission into evidence of an expert report through this process. And so we deleted it. Footnote -- footnote 88 was deleted, I believe, as a result of the court's order of last week. Finally, there are a small group of documents which have a different 65 ter number. It's the same document with a different 65 ter number and I'll explain why that happened. It's -- but first let me tell you what the documents are. It's 1996, 2006, 1989, 1974, 1981, 1986, 1905 and 1910. Those numbers appear on annex 2, the annex 2 spreadsheet which is now in evidence. On this spreadsheet they have a different number, same document, different number and here is why: It's because some documents appear twice on our 65 ter list and when they uploaded the documents into the e-court system they would detect that and they would pick one of them and upload only one of them. So these numbers did not get uploaded but the same document with a different number got uploaded and so we have indicated what the new number is and that is on the new spreadsheet. Now, there are -- there is one question that I would like to put to the witness and that he can explain with respect to this new spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkkanen, if you look at item 25 on the spreadsheet, there is a reference to 65 ter Exhibit 1451. Interview with Milan Martic, BBC, Death of Yugoslavia. Below there is something new that appears on this spreadsheet, which is tape 1 of Martic interview for Death of Yugoslavia, BBC and translation. Can you explain why that's been included?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes. When I was writing this annex 1, there was at that time only a transcript of this interview at our disposal. So later, the fuller video of this interview was obtained by the OTP and that's the second tape 1 of the same interview. Basically the content is exactly the same except for the fact that in the latest version also questions are included that were excluded from the first version of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On how many tapes was this interview recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know because I was using only the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is there a possibility that there could be a tape 2 or subsequent tapes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, theoretically, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Practically? Judging by the content of tape 1, does it -- did it give you the impression that it is a complete interview or that it continues beyond tape 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a complete interview of this part of the tape, of the video, of the interview, so the interview is complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were there many parts of the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the whole programme of this BBC programme is a very long one so I don't remember whether Mr. Martic was interviewed on this tape or this programme or on several different occasions. I was referring only to this particular interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can actually provide more information on this topic if the Court desires that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From the bar?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. It's a -- I don't believe it's -- I don't think there is any problem with me explaining it. It would be apparent if it were provided to the Court. What happened is, as Mr. Kerkkanen said when he wrote the reference that's included in his report is to a transcript of the interview, the transcript only has the answers, does not have the questions. And it's just a transcript. After the report -- after Mr. Kerkkanen left and the report was completed, the Tribunal, the OTP, made a request to the BBC to get a tape of the interview or else a transcript which contained both the questions and the answers. What was made available to the OTP was a part 1 of the interview, the first part, and in video, and we have transcribed that first part. It is not the complete interview on video. So we have the complete interview, transcript with just answers, and we have part of the interview, video, questions, and answers transcript. And that is what is reflected here on the spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't have subsequent parts of the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No we tried everything possible and those parts have gone policing, those tapes have gone policing from the BBC for reasons we don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There were certainly other parts?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Certainly were, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, at this time I'd like to move into evidence the documents that have not already been admitted that are reflected on this revised spreadsheet, and as we've done before, what I would suggest is that we, I don't think it's necessary to go through each one and assign it a number. I've already spoken with the Court officer and this can be done outside of hours, the Court officer could assign each document a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the Court officer is in possession of those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: They are all in the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in connection with this submission from the OTP, the Defence wishes to give an objection in principle because so far, in examining the witness, it was established that he was not an eyewitness, and that he was not an expert witness. This leads to the following question. On the basis of what and how will the authenticity of the documents be established? And I mean the documents that are supposed tonne tendered through this document. To us as the Defence, it would be very important to receive guidance and instructions from this Trial Chamber because this situation is quite similar to a situation that existed in the Limaj case where the OTP tried to tender some documentation through their own OTP expert and the Trial Chamber in that case found that such documents would only be considered as a continuation of the opening statement of the OTP. The testimony of this witness has been dealt with here by the Prosecutor and we would like to receive guidance from the Trial Chamber as to how to deal with this witness and the documents that are attendant to his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Documents attendant to his testimony or documents that are mentioned in the spreadsheet that is sought to be tendered into evidence? I'm not quite sure what you're talking about, Mr. Milovancevic, because the documents that relate to the witness's testimony have already been admitted under the previous -- the previous bunch, 03646958. Are you referring to the new document now, this new spreadsheet? Is that what you mean to refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in addition to the documents that are contained in the spreadsheet and that have already been tendered into evidence, there is a number of documents that have not been tendered into evidence so far and that the Prosecutor has moved that they be admitted into evidence through this witness, and my submission had to do with these new documents. In essence, this witness is neither an eyewitness, a fact witness, nor an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand you, Mr. Milovancevic. I thought Mr. Whiting had indicated that where documents are not -- have not been admitted, they have been it has been indicated that these have not been admitted and you don't seek to have them admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Actually, what we seek is the admission of all the documents that have not already been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if I -- if the Court wishes, I could address counsel's objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Number one, with respect to Defence counsel I think the Trial Chamber has given very clear guidance both in its orders and its rulings in court as far as admissibility and authenticity. I think what's very clear from the Court's guidelines and its rulings is that ordinarily authenticity issues will go to weight, will not be a bar to admission, and I think it's fair to say that the Court has adopted what we think is an excellent practice of admitting the documents that are offered for admission and considering the weight of those documents later. I know that documents have been offered by both the Defence and the Prosecution where no witness, neither a fact witness nor an expert, has been able to authenticate the document in a way we are familiar with. In this respect this is no departure whatever from previous practice. It's completely consistent with previous practice. In fact the witness here has provided a basis for -- he has provided a basis for admission. It's not just throwing documents in, because he's provided information about the source of each document. And he has provided some information about authenticity in comparing these documents to all the 50 to 100.000 documents that he reviewed. Secondly with respect to the Limaj case, I happen to know what Defence counsel is talking about because I did that case and I led that witness that he's referring to, and counsel, with respect, is incorrect in what he says. In fact, what happened with the OTP investigator who was the first witness in the case, is the documents that he spoke about were admitted into evidence. What -- it was the comment of the witness that were considered by the Trial Chamber to be not expert witness comments or not fact-witness comments but just a guidance, just a helpful indication or as the Trial Chamber in that case put it, a continuation of the opening statement. In other words, a kinds of road map. And that is exactly what has happened in this case with the Rule 89 F statement. We have offered the Rule 89(F) statement quite clearly as just being a road map to these documents to assist the Trial Chamber in making sense of them. But it's the documents that are going to be the evidence and it's the documents that will speak for themselves. So on that basis, I think that the admission of these documents is warranted and fully consistent with the way we've been proceeding in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: With perhaps a little small exception, Mr. Whiting, and please do correct the Bench if I'm wrong, here it looks like we've been asked -- the Bench has been asked to admit documents, a list of those documents, not the actual documents themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I wasn't clear on that. What I wanted to -- I wanted to use this spreadsheet as a guide but I want to admit the actual documents themselves. Not the spreadsheet but the actual documents themselves. This is just to assist the Trial Chamber and most particularly the Court officer in seeing which documents go into evidence. But it's the documents themselves we want in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying and I'm saying that the Prosecution is using a spreadsheet, a list of those documents, to admit those documents. So that this witness, and the Court, does not seem to have seen the documents that are sought to be admitted into evidence. This is the distinction I think I see between your particular case now and what you refer to in the other cases, like the Limaj case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's true I have not pulled up each document and examined it in court. However, that was the purpose of the Rule 89(F) statement, because the Rule 89(F) statement discusses and cites each document so that process which we could have done in court, we could have -- I could go through and pull up each document, in order to save time we offered the Rule 89(F) statement which accomplishes that exact same purpose and, of course, the documents will be available to the Trial Chamber to examine one by one. The parties will have the opportunity to argue about those documents, about what they mean, how they relate to the events and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you to say that the actual documents yourself are annexes to the 89(F) statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. What's an annex to the 89(F) statement is the spreadsheet which lists the documents and their sources. And now, in order for the Trial Chamber to be able to evaluate the documents themselves, we need to move the documents themselves into evidence because, of course, this witness is not offered as an expert and we would not want the Court to rely, although I think what he says about the documents is accurate, he's not offered as an expert and we are not asking the courts to rely on his description. The Court can use that as guidance, as a road map, but I think the Court needs the documents themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Any reply to that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We stand by our objection, because we do not see that there has been an independent confirmation of the sources. Secondly, the documents can't speak for themselves. Thirdly, the Trial Chamber has not been made familiar with these documents. The Trial Chamber should become familiar with these documents through -- during the trial in order to be able to establish what their authenticity is or attach weight to them. And the gist of our objection is that this is not the way in our submission one ought to proceed in relation to these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But Mr. Milovancevic, the Trial Chamber is not going to attach authenticity and weight to those documents now during the trial. It is going to do that at a later stage when it assesses the entire evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our concern is the obligation of the Trial Chamber to assess the admissibility of documents during trial. Either of the sides have to tender a document to the Trial Chamber and then the Trial Chamber has to decide on its admissibility. That is what our objection is based on. In the situation as it is now, the Prosecution is offering an enormous number of documents without basically presenting them to the Trial Chamber. That is why we are objecting to that form of tendering documents, since the Trial Chamber did not have occasion to see the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: However, the Trial Chamber will have an opportunity to see those documents at some stage and assess the weight. I would imagine that there is a reason for this kind of procedure, Mr. Milovancevic, particularly given the completion strategy of the Tribunal. Otherwise we are going to spend hours here in court going through each document and admitting it individually when the Trial Chamber can assess it later. And obviously, the Defence always has the opportunity and the right, once it has already read through the documents, to object to any specific document in there that it wishes to do so. Is that not -- isn't that the practical procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In that case, the Defence will use its right and put questions to this witness which have to do with the documents mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Based on the guidelines on admission of documents into evidence, the documents are admitted into evidence. May they please be given exhibit numbers out of court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They shall, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkkanen, I'd like now to go through a small group of additional documents which were not cited in your report but which have relation to certain things that are discussed in your report. But before I start to do that, and I'm going to ask you with respect to each document what the source of the document is. Before I do that, could you tell us if you've done anything to prepare for this? In other words, have you -- for this part of the examination, what have you done to prepare?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: I had a possibility to see these documents, and to check from MIIF records the source of these documents, originals of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To check from what records?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From -- Your Honour, I was able to check from our OTP MIIF tracking system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: MIIF records.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: MIIF records, the origins of these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was a spreadsheet prepared with the description of these documents, their numbers, and the source as indicated on these MIIF records?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you review that spreadsheet and did you confirm the

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you review that spreadsheet and did you confirm the accuracy of the sources as indicated on that spreadsheet?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'd like to distribute -- provide to the witness and distribute to the Court and the parties this spreadsheet. Mr. Kerkkanen, is this the spreadsheet we were talking about?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes. This is the spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When we go through each document and discuss each document will you need this spreadsheet in order to tell us the source of each document?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes. I need this spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd like to look, please, at 65 ter Exhibit 630 -- I'm sorry, 432, but before I do that I'd like to go back to your report. On pages 34 and 46 of your report, do you talk about Captain Dragan in documents pertaining to his role in the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I could just have one moment, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are going to go through a series of documents and I had prepared copies, hard copies for the interpreters because they have asked to us have hard copies. But apparently they haven't made it into the interpreters and I would like them to have it. I see we're a little bit, a few minutes early for the break. I wonder if we could take the break just a few minutes early and I can make sure the interpreters can the hard copies. I can also provide a hard copy in both languages to the accused which will solve any problems that we might have with the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well, then. We'll take a short break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I proceed, just to be clear we've provided hard copies to the interpret force tore their assistance, and also, to the Defence counsel for the benefit of the accused, because as I understand it, with e-court when you have an English-speaking witness, the -- you cannot get B/C/S up on the accused's monitor. You can only get English because you have English for the witness so it's the same for the accused. So in order to remedy that -- that's not a problem for Defence counsel. It's only a problem for the accused but in order to remedy that we've provided hard copies of the documents in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkkanen, if you could look, please at the document on the screen and if we could scroll down a little bit, just -- and just for the record, this is 65 ter Exhibit 432. Can you tell us, Mr. Kerkkanen, what the date of this document is and what it is about?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Can you roll it up a little bit more?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Like that, you mean?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes. This document is from Ministry of the Defence of the Republic of Serbia dated the 20th of January 1992. Basically an answer to the national assembly of the Republic of Serbia concerning volunteers, including Captain Dragan, and this letter states that Captain Dragan has been training units in -- of the Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is the source of this document? How did the OTP obtain this document?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: According the MIIF record, this document has been obtained from the Serbian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would move this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 460, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkkanen, I want to refer now to page 51 of your report, and there you state that in fact it seems that Martic and his RS Krajina MUP units were deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina as of 10 June 1992. And then you go on to discuss some of the documents that show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at 65 ter Exhibit 2080? If we could just scroll down to give the witness an opportunity to see the document. Could we look at the next page of the document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkkanen, can you tell us what this document is, what its date is and what it is about?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Please, can you roll it a little bit down more? This document is from the RSK MUP, Ministry of Internal Affairs, to several Secretariats of Internal Affairs of the RSK, as well as for few police brigades of the RSK. Basically ordering them to move following the certain route to Bosnia, to Banja Luka, and the date of the document is 10th of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at the last page of the document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who is the document from, specifically?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: This document is from Mr. Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is the source of the document?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: The source of this document is Croatian state archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this document be moved into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 461, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we turn please to page 15 of your report? And in the last paragraph on that page in the English version you list some of the first police officers to serve in the Knin SUP and there are some names provided, for example, Dragan Karna, Goran Opacic, Ace Draca [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at 65 ter Exhibit 2152?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkkanen, could you take just a moment to look at that and then, when you're ready, tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Please can you take it a little more down? This document is a list of police personnel, MUP personnel, who were awarded by the RSK -- I don't now recall the name of this award but the medal or recognition on the security day of the RSK on the 5th of July but there is no year indicated in this document but as it speaks about the RSK, it can't be before 1992. So therefore the date must be between 1992 and 1995. And many of those persons listed in this document are the same that I have mentioned on the page 15 of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Mr. Kerkkanen, could you tell us what the source of this document is, please?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: This document is also from the Croatian state archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be moved into evidence and receive a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is received into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 462, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We spoke earlier in your testimony about references in your report to Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at 65 ter Exhibit 2327?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Kerkkanen, can you tell us what this document is, please, what the date is of the document and what it's about. If there is a date.

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: I don't see the date. Perhaps it's more further down. Yes, now I see. The date is 8th of November 1991, and this is a letter from Captain Dragan to the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Serbia in Belgrade, stating basically that he doesn't want to be called or to be just one of many reserve captains and he doesn't like that the [unintelligible] of Captain Dragan has been or will be downgraded and in addition to this, he refers to the Serbian State Security in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is the source of this document?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: This document -- this document has been provided to the OTP by Dr. Latgojic Glisic [phoen], who was chef de cabinet of Mr. Simovic in the Serbian Ministry of Defence in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence and receive a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is received into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 463, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at page 46 of your report? Do you talk about training at Golubic?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes. I do write about the training in Golubic in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter Exhibit 2349, please? Mr. Kerkkanen, can you tell us what this is, please?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: This document contains names of those from the region of -- or from the area of Knin municipality who finished their training at the Golubic training camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is the source of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: This document is also from the Croatian state archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence and receive a number, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 464, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could look at page 30 of your report, on page 30 and also on page 31, do you talk about a training centre at Samarica?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN
utterances.text: Yes. I talk about the training camp in Samarica in my report on page 30 and 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now at page 17 of your report, you also talk about Dvor Na Uni being under the control of the SAO Krajina Ministry of the Interior. Now, first of all, are you able to explain the name Dvor Na Uni, what that means?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could still on the subject of Dvor look at 65 ter Exhibit 2445, please. What is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN

utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING

utterances.speaker: ARI KERKKANEN

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
